intro: This course has met the Watchers, the giants, the gods of the nations and the council of heaven. Where do those ideas come from? This unit goes to the sources. It opens the ancient documents themselves: 1 Enoch and Jubilees, the Dead Sea Scrolls, Josephus and Philo, the tablets of Ugarit and the traditions of Mesopotamia. Then it listens to the researchers who have spent their careers reading them.

The first chapter reads the documents. You will see what 1 Enoch 6–16 says about the Watchers on Mount Hermon, how Jubilees retells the story with Mastema and his spirits, and what the broken Book of Giants adds. You will read how Josephus and Philo explained Genesis 6 to Greek readers, and compare the council of El at Ugarit with Psalm 82. You will also learn Samuel Sandmel's warning against overstating parallels.

The second chapter joins the conversation among scholars: Mullen and Smith on the divine council, the text critics on Deuteronomy 32:8, Milik, VanderKam and Nickelsburg on the date of 1 Enoch, Wright and Stuckenbruck on evil spirits, Reed on how the story traveled, Segal on two powers in heaven, and Heiser on the three rebellions. By the end you will be able to state an argument fairly and tell a settled claim from an open one.
bigQuestion: What do the primary documents say about the Watchers and the council of heaven, and how do researchers read them differently?

title: The Primary Documents and the Scholars

chapters.title: The Documents: Enoch, Jubilees, the Scrolls and Their Neighbors
chapters.bigQuestion: What do the ancient documents themselves say about the Watchers, the giants and the council of heaven, before anyone explains them?

story.title: The Plow That Opened a Library
story.kicker: In 1928 a farmer in northern Syria struck a stone, and a lost city began to speak again.
paragraphs: In the spring of 1928 a farmer was plowing a field near the Mediterranean coast of northern Syria, close to a bay called Minet el-Beida. His plow struck something hard. When he dug around it, he found a large stone slab. Under the slab was an old stone-built tomb, with pottery still inside. Local officials reported the find, and word reached archaeologists working for France, which governed Syria at the time.

The next year a French team led by Claude Schaeffer began digging at a mound nearby called Ras Shamra. Within weeks they found clay tablets covered in wedge-shaped marks. Some used the Akkadian script scholars already knew. Others used a script no one had seen before. It had only about thirty signs, which meant it was probably an alphabet.

By 1930 and 1931 several scholars had deciphered it. The language was close to Hebrew and was named Ugaritic, after the city. The mound was ancient Ugarit, a trading port destroyed around 1185 BCE. Its scribes had left letters, business records and long poems about gods. The poems told of a high god named El, who sat at the head of an assembly of gods called his sons.

Ugarit is only one of the libraries this chapter opens. Nineteen years after the plow struck stone, shepherds near the Dead Sea found the first of the Dead Sea Scrolls. Among them were Aramaic copies of the book of 1 Enoch, pieces of a lost Book of Giants, and a retelling of Genesis. Older still, Greek-speaking Jewish writers such as Philo and Josephus had written about the same stories.

This chapter reads those documents first, in their own words or in close paraphrase. It asks what each one says about the Watchers, the giants, the spirits and the council of heaven. Only after that does it turn to what researchers have made of them. The next chapter follows the researchers themselves.
story.think: Why might it matter to read an ancient text yourself before reading what a modern scholar says about it?

lessons.title: Five Books in One
lessons.mainIdea: 1 Enoch is a collection of five Jewish writings from about 300 BCE to the first century CE, kept whole in Ge'ez and found in part among the Dead Sea Scrolls.
reading: Genesis 5:21–24 says only a little about Enoch. He was the seventh in the line from Adam, he walked with God, and he was not, for God took him. Jewish writers in the centuries before Jesus filled that silence. They wrote books in Enoch's name about what he saw in heaven and what he learned about the world. Scholars call the collection *1 Enoch*.

1 Enoch has five main parts. The Book of the Watchers (chapters 1–36) tells of the angels who came down to earth. The Parables, or Similitudes (37–71), describe a heavenly figure called the Elect One and the Son of Man. The Astronomical Book (72–82) lays out a calendar of the sun and moon. The Dream Visions (83–90) retell history as animals in a dream. The Epistle of Enoch (91–108) gives teaching and warnings.

The whole book survives only in *Ge'ez*, the old church language of Ethiopia. It is part of the Bible of the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches. In 1773 the Scottish traveler James Bruce brought Ge'ez copies to Europe. Parts also survive in Greek. Then, from 1947 on, Aramaic fragments were found in the caves at Qumran, showing that the book was being copied before the time of Jesus.

This course quotes 1 Enoch from the English translation by R. H. Charles, reissued in a small edition in 1917 and now in the public domain. Modern translations, such as the one by George Nickelsburg and James VanderKam (2004), are more exact but still under copyright, so they are described rather than quoted.

lessons.title: The Watchers on Mount Hermon
lessons.mainIdea: 1 Enoch 6–11 tells how two hundred Watchers swore an oath on Mount Hermon, took human wives, fathered giants and taught forbidden skills, until God sent his angels to act.
reading: 1 Enoch 6 begins where Genesis 6:1–2 begins. People multiplied and beautiful daughters were born to them. Then the angels, the children of heaven, saw them and desired them. Their leader, whom Charles spells Semjaza, feared he alone would pay for the plan. So all of them swore an oath together. The text says there were two hundred, and they came down in the days of Jared on the summit of Mount *Hermon*.

Chapter 7 says the *Watchers* took wives and taught them charms and the cutting of roots and plants. The women bore great giants. The giants ate up all that people had grown, and then turned to violence against people and animals. Chapter 8 lists what one Watcher, *Azazel*, taught: how to make swords, knives, shields and armor, and how to make ornaments, bracelets and eye makeup. Other Watchers taught the signs of the stars and moon.

Chapters 9 and 10 turn to heaven. The archangels Michael, Uriel, Raphael and Gabriel look down and bring the cry of the earth before God. God sends a messenger to warn Noah of the flood. Raphael binds Azazel and places him in darkness. Gabriel sets the giants against one another. Michael binds Semjaza and his companions in the valleys of the earth until the day of judgment. Then the earth is cleansed and renewed.

Readers notice that this story is much longer than Genesis 6:1–4, which does not name the angels, count them, or mention Hermon. Many scholars also see two threads woven together here: one about Semjaza and the oath, and one about Azazel and his teaching. Chapter 30 looks at how researchers explain that.

a tall mountain at the north of ancient Israel where, in 1 Enoch 6, the Watchers swore their oath

a chief angel; 1 Enoch names Michael, Uriel, Raphael and Gabriel among them

lessons.title: Enoch's Errand and the Spirits
lessons.mainIdea: In 1 Enoch 12–16 Enoch carries a message of judgment to the Watchers, and God's answer says the spirits of the giants will remain on earth as evil spirits.
reading: In 1 Enoch 12, Enoch is called a scribe of righteousness. Holy angels send him to tell the Watchers that they will have no peace. The frightened Watchers ask Enoch to write a petition for them and carry it to God. Enoch reads it by the waters of Dan, south-west of Hermon, and falls asleep. In a vision he is taken up to a house of crystal and fire, where the Great Glory sits on a throne (chapter 14).

The answer comes in chapter 15. God tells Enoch to say to the Watchers that they should pray for humans, not humans for them. They were holy, spiritual and living forever, yet they left heaven and took wives. Then comes a claim about the giants. Because the giants were born of spirits and flesh, their spirits will be called *evil spirits* on the earth, and the earth will be their dwelling (15:8–10).

Chapter 16 adds that these spirits will go on troubling people, without being judged, until the day of the great judgment. This is one of the oldest Jewish explanations of where harmful spirits came from. It is a story about the origin of evil in the world, told with the language of angels and giants. It says nothing about any particular person being troubled by a spirit.

Researchers read this passage closely. Researchers such as Archie Wright and Loren Stuckenbruck have asked how it shaped later Jewish and Christian ideas of *unclean spirits*. Their readings are the subject of the next chapter. Here the first step is simply to know what chapter 15 says.

lessons.title: Jubilees: Teachers Who Fell
lessons.mainIdea: Jubilees retells Genesis and says the Watchers were first sent down to teach justice, and only later sinned with human women.
reading: The Book of *Jubilees* retells Genesis and the start of Exodus as a revelation to Moses on Mount Sinai. It arranges history in jubilees, periods of forty-nine years. Most scholars date it to the middle of the second century BCE. Over a dozen Hebrew copies were found at Qumran, and the full text survives in Ge'ez. Like 1 Enoch, it is part of the Ethiopian Orthodox Bible. This course uses R. H. Charles's translation (1917).

Jubilees 4:15 explains the name Jared. In his days the angels of the Lord, called the Watchers, came down to earth. The text says they were sent to teach humans and to do judgment and uprightness on the earth. That is a different beginning from 1 Enoch 6, where the Watchers come down already planning to take wives.

Jubilees 4:17–22 then praises Enoch. He was the first among humans to learn writing, knowledge and wisdom, and he wrote down the signs of heaven. He was with the angels for six jubilees of years. He testified against the Watchers, who sinned with the daughters of men. In Jubilees 5:1–11 the Watchers take wives, the giants are born, and wrongdoing spreads. God binds the Watchers in the depths of the earth and sends a sword among the giants, so that they destroy one another.

Putting the two books side by side shows how one story can be retold. Both describe a fall of heavenly beings and the birth of giants. But Jubilees stresses that the Watchers' mission began well. Readers often note that this makes the fall a turning away from a good task, not a plan from the start.

words.d: a Jewish retelling of Genesis and early Exodus from about the second century BCE, arranged in periods of forty-nine years
in the Book of Jubilees, a period of forty-nine years (seven times seven)
a new version of an older story that keeps its outline but adds, cuts or explains details

lessons.title: Mastema Asks for a Tenth
lessons.mainIdea: Jubilees 10:1–14 tells how evil spirits troubled Noah's grandchildren, Noah prayed, and God bound nine parts of them, leaving one tenth under a leader called Mastema.
reading: Jubilees 10 is set after the flood. The text says unclean *demons* began to lead Noah's grandchildren astray. Noah prays to God to shut them away, so that they cannot rule over the spirits of the living. He reminds God that these spirits are the offspring of the Watchers. God tells the angels to bind all of them.

Then a new figure speaks. *Mastema*, the chief of the spirits, asks God to leave some of them with him. He says that without them he cannot carry out his work among humans, because human wickedness is great. God agrees to leave one tenth of the spirits with Mastema and to send nine parts to the place of judgment. The chapter ends with Noah writing down what the angels taught him and giving his book to his son Shem.

The name Mastema is related to a Hebrew word for hostility. In Jubilees he acts somewhat like the *satan* figure of Job 1–2: a being who tests and accuses, but only with God's permission. Jubilees also gives him roles in later stories, such as testing Abraham. Readers see in this chapter an early attempt to explain why evil still exists after the flood, and why it has limits.

lessons.title: The Book of Giants
lessons.mainIdea: Fragments of an Aramaic Book of Giants, identified at Qumran by J. T. Milik and edited by Loren Stuckenbruck, tell the story from the giants' side.
reading: Among the Qumran fragments, scholars found pieces of an Aramaic book that tells the Watchers story from the point of view of the giants. It is now called the *Book of Giants*. The fragments are small and broken. Even so, they show two giants, Ohyah and Hahyah, troubled by dreams. In one dream, gardeners water a garden of trees, and then water and fire destroy it. The giants send one of their number, Mahway, to ask Enoch what the dreams mean.

The fragments also name *Gilgamesh*, the hero of the Mesopotamian epic, as one of the giants. That surprised scholars. It shows that Jewish writers in this period knew some Mesopotamian names and put them into their own story. A later version of the Book of Giants was used by the teacher Mani in the third century CE. Pieces of it were found in Central Asia, at Turfan, in the early 1900s.

J. T. Milik published Aramaic Enoch fragments in The Books of Enoch: Aramaic Fragments of Qumrân Cave 4 (1976). He identified the Qumran giants fragments with the book Mani's followers used. Loren Stuckenbruck later edited all the fragments with a translation and commentary in The Book of Giants from Qumran (1997). Because the fragments are broken, both scholars stressed that the order of scenes is partly a reconstruction.

words.d: an Aramaic book, known from Qumran fragments, that tells the Watchers story from the giants' point of view
the hero of an ancient Mesopotamian epic; his name appears among the giants in the Qumran fragments
a broken piece of a manuscript; scholars reconstruct books from many fragments

sections.title: Other Voices from the Same Centuries

lessons.title: Two Scroll Echoes
lessons.mainIdea: The Damascus Document names the Watchers who fell as a warning, and the Genesis Apocryphon imagines Lamech fearing that his son Noah was a Watcher's child.
reading: The *Damascus Document* was first found not at Qumran but in the storeroom of a Cairo synagogue, the Cairo Genizah. Solomon Schechter published it in 1910. Later, copies turned up in the Qumran caves. It gives rules and history for a Jewish community. In column 2 it warns its readers to walk in God's ways, and gives examples of those who did not.

The first example is the Watchers of heaven. The document says they fell because they walked in the stubbornness of their hearts and did not keep God's commandments. Their sons, it says, were as tall as cedars, with bodies like mountains, and they fell too. Here the Watchers story is not told at length. It is used in a short list of warnings, which shows the readers already knew it.

The *Genesis Apocryphon*, found in Cave 1 in 1947 and first published in 1956, retells Genesis in Aramaic. In one scene, Lamech sees his newborn son Noah and fears the child's father was one of the Watchers or holy ones. His wife, Bitenosh, swears that the child is his. Lamech still goes to his father Methuselah, who travels to Enoch to ask. 1 Enoch 106–107 tells a similar story about Noah's birth.

words.d: a rule book of a Jewish community, found in Cairo and later at Qumran, that names the Watchers who fell as a warning
a storeroom in a Cairo synagogue where worn-out writings were kept; many ancient texts were found there
an Aramaic retelling of Genesis found in Qumran Cave 1 in 1947

lessons.title: Josephus on Angels and Women
lessons.mainIdea: Josephus, writing in Rome around 93 CE, retold Genesis 6 for Greek readers and said that many angels of God joined with women and fathered sons like the Greek giants.
reading: *Josephus* was a Jewish priest and historian born in Jerusalem around 37 CE. After the Jewish war with Rome, he lived in Rome and wrote in Greek. His Jewish Antiquities, finished around 93 CE, retells Israel's history for Greek and Roman readers. William Whiston's English translation (1737) is in the public domain.

In Antiquities 1.73 (book 1, chapter 3 in Whiston), Josephus tells what happened after the generations of Seth. In Whiston's words, many angels of God accompanied with women. Their sons, he says, were unjust and scorned what was good, trusting their own strength. He adds that the tradition says these men did things like the acts of those the Greeks call giants.

Josephus stands at an interesting point. He reads the sons of God of Genesis 6 as angels, as 1 Enoch and Jubilees do. But he does not tell the longer story of the Watchers, Hermon or the spirits. He also compares the sons to the giants of Greek stories, so his readers would understand. Scholars note that this comparison is Josephus's own bridge between two cultures, not a claim that the stories are the same.

Josephus's history of the Jewish people from creation to his own day

lessons.title: Philo, On the Giants
lessons.mainIdea: Philo of Alexandria read the angels of Genesis 6 as real souls in the air, but he also read the passage as an allegory about the soul and its choices.
reading: *Philo* was a Jewish thinker in Alexandria, Egypt, who lived from about 20 BCE to about 50 CE. He wrote in Greek and read the Bible in the Greek translation called the *Septuagint*. He wrote a short treatise on Genesis 6:1–4 called On the Giants. C. D. Yonge's English translation (1854–55) is in the public domain.

The Greek text Philo quoted reads angels of God in Genesis 6:2, not sons of God. The Septuagint also renders the Hebrew Nephilim of verse 4 with the Greek word gigantes, giants. Philo says that the beings other philosophers call daimones, Moses calls angels. They are souls that live in the air. Some serve God as messengers. Others, he says, are drawn down toward the body.

Philo then reads the passage as an *allegory*, a story whose parts stand for ideas. In his reading, the giants stand for people who live only for bodily pleasure, the earth-born. Others are born of heaven, living by the mind, or born of God, like priests and prophets. So Philo holds two readings at once: angels exist, and the story also teaches about the soul. Many ancient readers of the Bible did the same.

lessons.title: The Council of El
lessons.mainIdea: Ugaritic poems from about 1400–1185 BCE picture El leading an assembly of the gods, and scholars compare that picture with Psalm 82 and Psalm 29.
reading: Most tablets from *Ugarit* date from about 1400 to 1185 BCE, centuries before most dates scholars give for the written books of the Hebrew Bible. In the poems, El is the aged king and father of the gods. The gods gather around him in an assembly. The tablets use phrases meaning the assembly of the gods and the circle of the sons of El. Scholars call such a gathering a *divine council*. One poem also mentions the seventy sons of Athirat, El's wife.

Psalm 82:1, in the King James Version, reads: God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods. The Hebrew for congregation of the mighty is adat el, which can be translated the council of El. Psalm 29 opens by calling on the bene elim, the sons of God or heavenly beings, to give glory to the LORD. It then describes the LORD's voice thundering over the waters, much as Ugaritic poems describe the storm god Baal.

Most scholars agree that council language appears both at Ugarit and in the Bible. They differ on what it means. E. Theodore Mullen compared the two in detail in his 1980 study. Mark S. Smith has argued that Israel's faith grew out of this Canaanite setting. Michael Heiser, whose 2004 dissertation studied the divine council, argued that biblical writers used the shared vocabulary to make their own claim: Israel's God rules the council. Chapter 30 follows that debate.

lessons.title: The Apkallu and Oannes
lessons.mainIdea: Mesopotamian tradition honored seven wise apkallu before the flood, and Amar Annus (2010) compared them with the Watchers, who in 1 Enoch bring knowledge that causes harm.
reading: In Mesopotamian tradition the *apkallu* were seven wise beings who lived before the great flood. They were said to have brought people the arts of civilization, such as writing, building and crafts. Assyrian palace carvings from the 800s BCE show figures often identified as apkallu, some in a fish-shaped cloak and some with a bird's head. Kings liked to link their own wisdom to these sages.

*Berossus*, a Babylonian priest writing in Greek around 290 BCE, told of a being called *Oannes*. Oannes came up out of the sea, part fish and part man, and taught humans letters, sciences and crafts. His history survives only in quotations by later writers. Even so, it shows how the apkallu tradition was being told to Greek readers in the same centuries that the Book of the Watchers was being written.

In 2010 Amar Annus published On the Origin of Watchers in the Journal for the Study of the Pseudepigrapha. He compared the apkallu with the Watchers of 1 Enoch. In Mesopotamia, bringing knowledge made the sages heroes. In 1 Enoch 8, heavenly teachers bring knowledge, such as weapon-making, that leads to harm. Annus read the Jewish story as reversing the Mesopotamian one. Heiser drew on the same comparison in Reversing Hermon (2017). Other scholars think both traditions grew from a shared stock of flood-era stories.

lessons.title: Beware of Parallelomania
lessons.mainIdea: Samuel Sandmel coined parallelomania in 1961 for overstating likenesses between texts, a warning that applies to every comparison in this chapter.
reading: In December 1961 Samuel Sandmel, a Jewish scholar of the New Testament and early Judaism, gave the presidential address to the Society of Biblical Literature. It was published the next year under the title Parallelomania. He used the word to name a habit in scholarship: finding a likeness between two texts, overstating it, and then claiming one copied the other, as if the direction of borrowing were obvious.

Sandmel did not say comparison is useless. He said a likeness is only the start of the work. A shared image might come from a shared culture, from a common older source, or from chance. And the same phrase can mean something different in each text. This chapter has placed many texts side by side: Enoch and Jubilees, Genesis and Josephus, Ugarit and the Psalms, the apkallu and the Watchers. Each pairing needs that care.

The caution also guards against sensational claims. Some popular books say Mesopotamian carvings show ancient astronauts, or that giants built the pyramids. The texts say nothing of the kind. Researchers of many views reject such claims. Michael Heiser, for example, publicly challenged Zecharia Sitchin, arguing that Sitchin's readings did not match the actual Sumerian and Akkadian words.

words.d: Samuel Sandmel's 1961 word for overstating likenesses between texts and assuming one borrowed from the other
a likeness between two texts, such as a shared phrase, image or story pattern
the effect one text or culture has on another; scholars must show it, not assume it

chapters.title: Scholars in Conversation
chapters.bigQuestion: When careful researchers read the same ancient documents and reach different conclusions, how can a student weigh their arguments fairly?

story.title: Two Stacks of Books
story.kicker: Two students read the same psalm, pile up commentaries by different scholars, and have to write one paper together.
paragraphs: It is late on a weekday evening in a university library. Two students, Dana and Marcus, share a long table near the reference shelves. Between them lies an open Bible, turned to Psalm 82. They are writing a joint paper for a class on the Psalms. They cannot agree on the first sentence.

Dana has stacked up books on the ancient Near East: E. Theodore Mullen's study of the divine council, Mark S. Smith's The Origins of Biblical Monotheism, and Michael Heiser's The Unseen Realm. She taps verse 1. God stands in the council of El, she says, and judges among the gods. That phrase has a known meaning at Ugarit. And verse 7 says they will die like humans. You say that only to someone who is not human.

Marcus has a different stack: older commentaries, a volume of Rashi in English, and a book of rabbinic readings. One reads the gods as judges in Israel, called gods because they judged in God's name. He points to John 10:34, where Jesus quotes the psalm. Some interpreters read Jesus as speaking about human leaders there. Then he slides over a third book that reads the psalm as spoken to Israel at Mount Sinai.

Dana writes three words across the top of a notepad: claim, evidence, counter-evidence. Under claim she writes her reading and his. Under evidence each of them lists verses, manuscripts and parallels. Under counter-evidence each has to write the strongest point against their own view. Marcus groans, then laughs, and starts writing.

By closing time the paper still has two readings, but each one is stated fairly. They have also noticed that their authors agree on some things, such as what the Hebrew words say, and argue about others. This chapter follows the researchers who study these texts, and maps where they agree and where they part ways.
story.think: Why might writing the strongest point against your own view make your paper better?

lessons.title: From Ugarit to the Psalms
lessons.mainIdea: Scholars such as Frank Moore Cross and E. Theodore Mullen studied the divine council decades before popular books made it widely known.
reading: The Hebrew Bible has several scenes set in a heavenly court. In 1 Kings 22:19–22 the prophet Micaiah sees the LORD on his throne with the host of heaven around him, discussing a plan. Job 1–2 opens with the sons of God presenting themselves before the LORD. In Isaiah 6 the prophet hears the question, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Psalm 82 names the council outright.

After the Ugaritic tablets were read in the 1930s, scholars could compare these scenes with the assembly of El. Frank Moore Cross discussed the council in Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic (1973). E. Theodore Mullen gave it a full study in The Assembly of the Gods: The Divine Council in Canaanite and Early Hebrew Literature (1980). He set the Ugaritic assembly beside the council scenes of the Hebrew Bible and traced what was shared and what was changed.

So the idea of a *divine council* is not the view of one writer. It is a standard topic in the study of the Hebrew Bible. Most scholars agree the texts use council imagery. What they debate is what that imagery meant to Israel's writers, and whether it changed over time. The next lessons follow that debate.

a biblical phrase for the heavenly beings around God's throne, as in 1 Kings 22:19

lessons.title: One God and the Council
lessons.mainIdea: Mark S. Smith reads Israel's monotheism as developing over time, while Michael Heiser read the canon as one God above a council of lesser beings.
reading: Isaiah 45:5 has God say: I am the LORD, and there is none else, there is no God beside me (KJV). Yet Psalm 82 and Deuteronomy 32 speak of gods or sons of God. How do these fit together? Scholars who study the history of Israel's religion give different answers. The question involves dating texts, reading Ugarit, and deciding what an ancient writer meant by a god.

Mark S. Smith is a leading scholar of Ugarit and the Hebrew Bible. In The Early History of God (1990) and The Origins of Biblical Monotheism (2001), he argues that Israel's religion grew over centuries from a Canaanite setting. In his view, clear statements of *monotheism*, the belief that only one god exists, come in texts from around the Babylonian exile, such as Isaiah 40–55.

Michael Heiser, in his 2004 dissertation and later The Unseen Realm (2015), read the texts as they stand in the canon. He argued they show one God who is unlike all others, with a council of lesser *elohim* he created. He read Isaiah 45:5 as a claim that none compares with the LORD, not a denial that other heavenly beings exist. Smith and many others read such verses as denying that other gods exist. Each reading takes the Hebrew seriously; they differ on method.

lessons.title: Deuteronomy 32:8 and the Text Critics
lessons.mainIdea: A Dead Sea Scroll and the Septuagint point to sons of God in Deuteronomy 32:8, a reading most text critics now accept over the Masoretic sons of Israel.
reading: Deuteronomy 32:8 in the King James Version reads: When the most High divided to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel. That last phrase follows the *Masoretic Text*, the standard Hebrew text behind most Bibles.

A copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran, called 4QDeut j, is centuries older than the oldest complete Masoretic manuscripts. At this verse it reads sons of God. The *Septuagint* points the same way; most of its copies read angels of God. To choose between readings, text critics ask which one best explains how the others arose. A scribe is more likely to smooth a puzzling phrase than to create one. Many judge that sons of God was changed to sons of Israel, not the reverse.

This method is called *textual criticism*. Emanuel Tov's handbook, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible (first English edition 1992), sets out its tools. Several modern translations now follow the scroll here. Scholars with very different views accept this reading, among them Smith and Heiser, who argued for it in a 2001 journal article. Some still defend sons of Israel, linking it to the seventy of Jacob's family in Genesis 46:27.

lessons.title: Milik and the Cave 4 Fragments
lessons.mainIdea: J. T. Milik's 1976 edition of the Aramaic Enoch fragments showed that most of 1 Enoch was being copied by about 200 BCE, though not the Parables.
reading: Before 1947, scholars knew 1 Enoch mainly from Ge'ez manuscripts and some Greek pieces. Many dated its parts to the second or first century BCE. Then the Qumran caves gave up Aramaic fragments. J. T. Milik, a Polish scholar on the team that worked on the Cave 4 scrolls, published them in The Books of Enoch: Aramaic Fragments of Qumrân Cave 4 (1976).

Milik's edition showed copies of the Book of the Watchers, the Astronomical Book, the Dream Visions and the Epistle. He dated some of the oldest copies, including one of the Astronomical Book and one of the Book of the Watchers, to around 200 BCE or a little after. If a book was already being copied then, it must have been written earlier. This pushed the oldest parts of 1 Enoch back into the third century BCE.

One part was missing: the Parables (chapters 37–71). Milik argued that the Parables were a much later Christian work, from around 270 CE. Most scholars have not followed that date. Many now place the Parables around the turn of the era, in the first century BCE or first century CE. The debate shows how a new *manuscript* find can settle one question and open another.

lessons.title: VanderKam and the Seventh from Adam
lessons.mainIdea: James VanderKam (1984) traced how the Enoch tradition grew, and compared Enoch, seventh from Adam, with Enmeduranki, the seventh king before the flood in Mesopotamian lists.
reading: Genesis 5 places Enoch seventh in the line from Adam and gives him 365 years, the number of days in a solar year. It says he walked with God. James VanderKam, in Enoch and the Growth of an Apocalyptic Tradition (1984), asked why Jewish writers built so much on so few lines.

VanderKam pointed to Mesopotamian lists of kings who ruled before the flood. The seventh, Enmeduranki, was linked to the sun god and to secret knowledge about reading the future. VanderKam argued that Jewish writers knew such traditions. They shaped Enoch as a Jewish answer: the seventh man, linked to the sun's year, who received true knowledge from God's angels rather than from divination.

VanderKam also traced the order of the Enoch books. He treated the Astronomical Book and the Book of the Watchers as the oldest, from the third century BCE, with later parts added over time. That is why scholars speak of the growth of the Enoch tradition. Later, VanderKam and George Nickelsburg together published 1 Enoch: A New Translation (2004), now widely used by students.

lessons.title: Nickelsburg's Commentary
lessons.mainIdea: George Nickelsburg's commentary (2001) reads 1 Enoch 6–11 as two woven strands and has suggested that the giants' violence reflects the wars of its own time.
reading: George W. E. Nickelsburg's 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary (Hermeneia, 2001) covers chapters 1–36 and 81–108 verse by verse. It is one of the most detailed studies of the Book of the Watchers. Like many scholars, Nickelsburg sees in chapters 6–11 two strands woven together. In one, Shemihazah leads the Watchers, who take wives and father giants. In the other, Asael (called Azazel in Charles's translation) teaches forbidden arts.

Nickelsburg has also asked why such a story would be told when it was. After Alexander the Great died in 323 BCE, his generals fought long wars over his empire, and the land of Israel lay between them. Nickelsburg has suggested that the giants, who claim descent from heavenly beings and fill the earth with violence, mirror those warring rulers. Some Greek kings in this period did claim divine descent.

Other scholars stress different settings, such as disputes among priests or the pull of Greek learning. A reader can hold these views side by side. Each asks what the story meant to its first hearers. None of them requires a reader to decide whether Watchers existed. That question belongs to faith communities, not to the historian's method.

lessons.title: Where Unclean Spirits Come From
lessons.mainIdea: Archie Wright, Loren Stuckenbruck and Michael Heiser have each traced how 1 Enoch 15's giant spirits shaped later ideas of unclean spirits, while other readers see demons as fallen angels.
reading: The Gospels speak of *unclean spirits*. In Mark 1:23–27, in the synagogue at Capernaum, a man cries out, and Jesus commands the unclean spirit to leave. The man is a member of that town and that synagogue, and the story ends with him free and the crowd amazed. The Gospels do not explain where such spirits came from. Researchers have asked what background their first readers had.

Archie T. Wright, in The Origin of Evil Spirits (2005), studied how early Jewish writers received Genesis 6:1–4. He argued that the Book of the Watchers, with its giant spirits in chapter 15, shaped later Jewish thinking about evil spirits. Loren Stuckenbruck's essays in The Myth of Rebellious Angels (2014) also trace how the Watchers and giants traditions were used in Second Temple texts and the New Testament.

Michael Heiser, in The Unseen Realm (2015) and Demons (2020), held that demons in the Gospels are the spirits of the dead giants, following 1 Enoch 15. Many Christian readers through history have instead understood demons as fallen angels themselves, cast out of heaven with Satan. Both readings appear among careful scholars. None of these researchers linked unclean spirits to illness, disability or how a person's mind works.

lessons.title: How the Watchers Story Traveled
lessons.mainIdea: Annette Yoshiko Reed (2005) traced how the Watchers story was embraced by early Christian writers, set aside by most rabbis, and later replaced in much of the church by the Sethite reading.
reading: Jude 14–15 quotes a prophecy of Enoch that closely matches 1 Enoch 1:9. Early Christian writers used the Watchers story too. Justin Martyr, writing in Rome around 150 CE, said in his Second Apology that angels broke God's order, loved women and fathered children who are called demons. Tertullian, around 200 CE, defended the book of Enoch as Scripture in On the Apparel of Women, though he knew some did not accept it.

Annette Yoshiko Reed traced this history in Fallen Angels and the History of Judaism and Christianity (2005). She showed that the Watchers story was widely read in the Second Temple period. Then, in different ways, both rabbinic Judaism and much of the Christian church moved it to the edges. Rabbinic sources such as Genesis Rabbah read the sons of God as sons of judges or nobles. Only the Ethiopian church kept 1 Enoch in its Bible.

In the church, the *Sethite view* spread. It reads the sons of God as the godly line of Seth and the daughters of men as the line of Cain. Julius Africanus held it in the early 200s. Augustine discussed it in The City of God in the early 400s. Many Protestant commentators have held it since. Reed's work helps readers see that a story's place in a tradition can change over centuries.

lessons.title: Two Powers in Heaven
lessons.mainIdea: Alan Segal (1977) studied rabbinic warnings against belief in two powers in heaven, and Heiser argued that the pattern behind that belief goes back to the Hebrew Bible.
reading: Daniel 7:9–14 describes a throne scene. The Ancient of Days takes his seat, and one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and receives everlasting rule. In Exodus 3 the angel of the LORD appears in the bush, and then God speaks from it. In Exodus 23:20–21 God says his name is in the angel he sends. Ancient readers asked how these figures relate to God.

In 1977 Alan Segal published Two Powers in Heaven: Early Rabbinic Reports about Christianity and Gnosticism. He studied rabbinic passages that warn against people who say there are two powers in heaven. Segal argued that the idea was older than the warnings. It grew from how some Jews read passages like Daniel 7, and the rabbis came to treat it as a serious error.

Heiser built on Segal in his dissertation (2004) and The Unseen Realm (2015). He argued that the Hebrew Bible itself has a visible and an invisible LORD figure, and that early Christians read Jesus into that pattern. Rabbinic Judaism reads these passages differently. The *Shema*, Deuteronomy 6:4, declares that the LORD is one. The angel of the LORD is read as a created messenger speaking in God's name.

lessons.title: A Framework and Its Critics
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser joined Genesis 3, 6 and 11 into three rebellions and a Deuteronomy 32 worldview; readers find it clarifying or too tightly systematized.
reading: Genesis 3 tells of the serpent in Eden. Genesis 6:1–4 tells of the sons of God and the daughters of men. Genesis 11 tells of Babel and the scattering of the nations. In the Bible these are separate stories. Heiser, in The Unseen Realm (2015), read them as three rebellions: in Eden, before the flood, and at Babel.

He tied the third to Deuteronomy 32:8–9, read with the Qumran scroll. In his view, after Babel God placed the nations under members of his council and kept Israel as his own. Psalm 82 then shows those rulers judged for ruling unjustly. Heiser called this the *Deuteronomy 32 worldview*. He used it to read Daniel 10's princes of Persia and Greece and Paul's language of rulers and authorities.

Other readers raise questions. Genesis does not call Babel a rebellion in heaven, and Deuteronomy 32:8 does not say the sons of God rebelled. Psalm 82 does not say when their wrongdoing began. Some reviewers say the framework joins texts from different books and centuries into a tighter system than any one of them states. Supporters reply that it explains passages that otherwise seem scattered. Christian tradition has more often spoken of one fall of angels and one fall of humanity.

lessons.title: Jewish Readings Through Time
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish readers of Genesis 6 moved from angels in 1 Enoch, Jubilees and Philo to rulers and judges in the Targum, Genesis Rabbah and Rashi.
reading: There is no single Jewish view of Genesis 6. Books written by Jews in the Second Temple period, such as 1 Enoch and Jubilees, read the sons of God as angels. So did Philo and Josephus in the first century CE. Some Dead Sea Scrolls, such as the Damascus Document, speak of the Watchers who fell.

Later rabbinic tradition mostly took another path. The *Targum* Onkelos, an Aramaic translation of the Torah, renders sons of God in Genesis 6:2 as sons of the great ones, meaning nobles. The *midrash* Genesis Rabbah reads it as sons of judges. Rashi, the great commentator of the eleventh century, explains them as sons of princes and judges. In this line, the wrong in Genesis 6 is the abuse of power by the mighty.

Jewish tradition still has a heavenly court. Genesis Rabbah, on Genesis 1:26, pictures God consulting the ministering angels before creating humans. What rabbinic Judaism rejects is a second being sharing God's rule. Today Jewish communities read these passages in many ways. A fair study notes the variety and does not treat any one period as the whole of Jewish reading.

lessons.title: Claim, Evidence, Counter-Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: A fair reader states each claim plainly, lists its evidence and its hardest counter-evidence, and sorts what is widely agreed from what is still debated.
reading: Every interpretation makes a *claim*. The claim should fit in one sentence so it can be tested: The gods in Psalm 82 are members of a heavenly council. Or: The gods in Psalm 82 are human judges. Next comes *evidence*: a verse, a word, a manuscript, a parallel. For the council reading, evidence includes adat el in verse 1, the Ugaritic parallels and die like men in verse 7.

Then comes *counter-evidence*, the facts hardest for the claim to explain. For the council reading, a reader might cite John 10:34–35, where Jesus speaks of those to whom the word of God came. For the human-judges reading, the council setting and die like men are the hardest facts. Stating the case against your own view is not weakness. It makes a conclusion trustworthy. Some teachers call this *steelmanning*.

Last comes sorting. Widely agreed: the Bible has council scenes; the Qumran scroll reads sons of God in Deuteronomy 32:8; Jude 14–15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9; most of 1 Enoch is older than 150 BCE. Still debated: how monotheism developed, where demons come from, the three rebellions, the date of the Parables. Keeping the lists apart prevents a common mistake: treating a debated claim as settled, or a settled one as mere opinion.
